K2 also records the ordering law that makes withholding safe and its one real consequence: the macOS default group moves from the shared literal to the app-ID literal, which TASK-260715-379cpk must be authored against. F3: com.apple.security.application-groups is now PROHIBITED on ios.probe.host and ios.probe.provider, because TASK-260715-1jckn0 scopes the probe to the NETunnelProviderManager lifecycle and versioned app messaging and names no shared container; G4 gains an explicit probeRule saying a probe inherits identifiers and profile classes but never entitlements. F2: TASK-260728-q5kjta's scope and AC4 were corrected on the board to name the same four macOS App IDs, Network Extensions only, zero App Group records and capabilities, no Keychain portal mutation, the Mac Development profile class, and all four excluded iOS App IDs. revisionLog.verifiedIndependently: Both findings were re-checked before being accepted. networkExtensionRule.statement: The com.apple.developer.networking.networkextension entitlement is carried by BOTH the containing app and the embedded provider. Its value depends on the SIGNING CHANNEL, not on the role and not on the packaging alone: direct Developer ID signing uses the values with the '-systemextension' suffix; every other channel — App Store distribution AND development signing — uses the values without that suffix.
networkExtensionRule.source: Apple DTS, https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/800887 — 'When you build an app with an embedded NE extension, both the app and the extension must be signed with the com.apple.developer.networking.networkextension entitlement. This is a restricted entitlement, that is, it must be authorised by a provisioning profile.' and 'The value of this entitlement is an array, and the values in that array differ depend on your distribution channel: If you distribute your app directly with Developer ID signing, use the values with the -systemextension suffix. Otherwise - including when you distribute the app on the App Store and when signing for development - use the values without that suffix.'
networkExtensionRule.profileWarning: Apple DTS, same source: 'Make sure you authorise these values with your provisioning profile. If, for example, you use an App Store distribution profile with a Developer ID signed app, things won't work because the profile doesn't authorise the right values.' The profile class and the entitlement value must therefore agree, which is why every value in this contract is keyed by channel.
networkExtensionRule.empiricalEvidence: Observed 2026-07-28 on this Mac with `codesign -d --entitlements :-`. Three shipping Developer-ID-distributed packet-tunnel products carry the suffixed value on BOTH the containing app and the embedded system extension: Tailscale (io.tailscale.ipn.macsys and .network-extension), PureVPN (com.purevpn.app.mac with .wireguard-packet-tunnel and com.purevpn.mac.packet-tunnel), Surfshark (com.surfshark.vpnclient.macos.direct and .PacketTunnel-WireGuard). appGroupStyleRule.rationale: Apple distinguishes two App Group ID styles. An iOS-style ID begins 'group.', is allocated on the Developer website, and is authorised by a provisioning profile. A macOS-style ID begins with the Team ID and CANNOT be explicitly allocated on the Developer website. Since 21 Feb 2025 iOS-style App Group IDs are fully supported on macOS for all product types, and Xcode 16.3 and later make the iOS style the macOS default. This project is new and builds with Xcode 26.5, so it takes the current, registrable style on both platforms. A team-prefixed macOS literal would not identify the portal record this contract says it consumes, which is the defect this revision closes.

Specifically, it's now possible to create a Mac provisioning profile that authorises the use of an iOS-style app group ID.' / 'With Xcode 16.3, it's now the default for macOS as well.' / on macOS-style IDs: 'It can't be explicitly allocated on the Developer website.' / 'If you're writing new code that uses app groups, use an iOS-style app group ID.'

appGroupPurposeRule.iOS: A genuinely shared filesystem container and UserDefaults suite. The host publishes the non-secret profile snapshot; the appex reads it. Host and appex run as the same user in the same context. Granted to the two PRODUCTION iOS targets, ios.host and ios.provider. Consumer: TASK-260715-3f4lxy.
appGroupPurposeRule.macOS: No function, therefore no grant. The provider runs as root, so its group container resolves under /private/var/root while the host's resolves under the logged-in user's home; the two never meet. The macOS host-to-provider channel selected by TASK-260728-7ii1xz is providerConfiguration for non-secret state plus a sendProviderMessage seed into a provider-owned system-domain keychain item, and the XPC candidate that would have needed a group-prefixed Mach name was rejected. com.apple.security.application-groups is prohibited on all four macOS targets under rule G4.

exceptionEntitlementRule.conditionalExceptionPolicy: A conditional entry is REVIEWED BUT NOT GRANTED. It is disjoint from reviewedExceptions by construction: reviewedExceptions is the ACTIVE register and must equal the set of temporary exceptions the target rows actually author, which is what rule R26 enforces and what keeps the active register honest. A conditional entry authors nothing, appears in no allowlist, moves no count, and must be ABSENT from every signed bundle while armed is false. Its purpose is narrow and is the point of the whole construction: the spec bans an UNREVIEWED exception entitlement, so an exception that a supported OS turns out to require must already have been reviewed, or the correct requirement gets rejected as drift the day the evidence arrives. crossPlatformSharingContract.statement: A cross-platform summary sentence carries NO independent authority. Every grant it states is DERIVED from the target rows and from the record lists, and rule R32 recomputes the derivation and compares it against the sentence before the contract is allowed to pass. A summary may not name a target as a grantee unless the target row grants it, and may not name a target at all unless the mention is registered below as a declared non-grantee contrast.
crossPlatformSharingContract.history: Reviewer verdict 05 F1. Through r5 the cross-platform summary was six free-text strings that nothing checked. r5 corrected eight target rows, two rules, two assertions and the C1 scope, and left crossPlatformRules[2] asserting the superseded r4 contract - that the shared Keychain access group is granted to the macOS host. The 846-check r5 validator passed, because no rule looked at the summary at all. The defect class is a prose summary that ASSERTS a grant set instead of RENDERING one; the fix is to make every such sentence a checked projection of the data rather than a second, unsynchronised statement of it.
crossPlatformSharingContract.mechanism: Each entry in crossPlatformRules has exactly one structured rule here, addressed by renderedIndex. The structured rule names the entitlement key it summarises; R32 derives the granted target set from the target rows, compares it with grantedTargets, compares that in turn with the record's own consumedByTargets, and then checks the prose: the grantClause must appear VERBATIM in the rendered sentence, the display names inside the grantClause must be exactly the granted targets, and every other target named anywhere in the sentence must appear in nonGranteeMentions with its own clause present verbatim. A stale sentence therefore fails on the clause, on the mention, or on both.
crossPlatformSharingContract.displayNameDerivation: A target's display name is derived from its own row - platform label ('iOS' or 'macOS'), then ' probe' for the probe family, then the role. macos.host is 'macOS host', ios.probe.provider is 'iOS probe provider'. R32 also treats the raw target key as a mention, so 'macos.host' and 'the macOS host' are both caught. No display name is a substring of another, so the scan cannot mis-attribute a mention.
crossPlatformSharingContract.authorityNote: grantClause is normative and machine-checked. The remaining prose in a rendered sentence is explanatory and carries no grant: it may not introduce a target that is not either a grantee or a declared non-grantee mention, which is the only way explanatory prose could smuggle a grant back in.
crossPlatformSharingContract.recordCountClaimRule: A sentence that states how many App Group records exist is a count claim. R32 scans every string in this contract for one, and every hit must sit at a path listed in recordCountClaimPaths with a number equal to the actual record count. That is what closes the second half of the class: r5 deleted the probe record and left two sentences still saying 'one record per family', which was true of r4's two-record world and false of r5's one-record world.
crossPlatformSharingContract.historicalPathsNote: These paths describe the state of an EARLIER revision on purpose and are pinned to it, so a count they mention is not a claim about the current data. Everything else is scanned. The exclusion list is declared here rather than hard-coded in the validator, so widening it is a visible edit to the contract.

authorizationNodeContract.revisionPinRule: The node's live contract fields must contain the rendered revisionPhrase for the current revision, and must contain NO superseded revision label. authorizationNodeContract.digestAlternativeRejected: Verdict 06 offered a content digest plus revision as an alternative pin. assertionScopeContract.statement: An assertion carries NO independent authority over WHICH targets or profiles it applies to. Every scope an assertion states is DERIVED from the authoritative rows — the target rows for an entitlement claim, the profile rows for a profile claim — and rules R35 and R36 recompute the derivation three ways and compare it against the assertion's own words before the contract is allowed to pass. An assertion may not claim a target it does not hold, may not omit one it does, and may not name a target at all unless the mention is registered below.
assertionScopeContract.history: Reviewer verdict 07. r6 closed exactly this defect class for the cross-platform summary (rule S1) and left the assertion list — the OTHER prose projection of the same rows — unchecked. Two assertions had already gone stale under it. A5 said application-groups is present on every iOS bundle, which r5 had made false for the iOS probe pair and which A18 directly contradicted; following A5 would have over-entitled both disposable probes. A9 said every development profile carries this Mac, which is false for the four iOS development profiles whose devices are deferred under ADR-024. The 1024-check r7 validator passed because R27 checked assertion MEMBERSHIP and substrings, never semantic scope against the rows. A third instance was found while fixing these two and is recorded in staleClaimsFound.
assertionScopeContract.mechanism: Each scope-bearing assertion has one entry here per polarity. Each entry declares classPredicates over the authoritative rows, and the SET those predicates select must equal the entry's declared scopeTargets, which must in turn equal the set the row STATUSES imply for that entitlement key and polarity. Three independent derivations of the same set: a predicate typo, a stale hand-written list, and a moved row each break a different one. The entry's scopeClause must then appear VERBATIM in the assertion text and again in the rationale document, and every target named anywhere in the assertion text must be either inside that assertion's scope or a declared nonScopeMention with its own clause present.
assertionScopeContract.polarityNote: present — the clause asserts the key is present on scopeTargets. absent — the clause asserts it is absent from scopeTargets. present-exclusive — the clause asserts presence on scopeTargets AND, through an explicit exclusivityMarker that must appear in the text, absence everywhere else; it therefore discharges the complement on its own and needs no paired absent entry. Choosing present-exclusive without the marker in the text is a failure, because 'present on X' alone says nothing about the rest.
assertionScopeContract.partitionRule: For every entitlement key registered here, the union of the present scopes must equal the set of target rows whose status for that key is an authored status, the union of the absent scopes (plus the complement discharged by any present-exclusive entry) must equal every remaining target row, and the two must be disjoint. A5 and A18 failed exactly this: their scopes OVERLAPPED on the two iOS probe rows, one claiming presence and the other absence, and nothing computed the union.
assertionScopeContract.coverageRule: Every entitlement key that appears literally in ANY assertion text must have at least one entry here, and every registered key must appear in the text of the assertion it is registered against. That is what makes the class fail closed rather than this one pair: a future assertion that names an entitlement key without registering its scope cannot pass R35, and a registered scope whose assertion stopped mentioning the key cannot either.
assertionScopeContract.profileScopeRule: A profile assertion is scoped the same way, over profiles[] rather than targets[]. deviceBinding declares what the profile rows must say about devices for the scope to be honest: 'enumerated' requires a concrete device list on every profile in scope, 'deferred' requires every device entry on every profile in scope to carry both the deferral marker and the deferral basis, and 'all-devices' is the distribution-channel form that provisions every device instead of listing any. The development-channel entries must partition the profile rows, and the enumerated set must equal the set of profiles Ceremony C1 authorizes — which is the tie that keeps A9a and the C1 scope from drifting apart.
assertionScopeContract.deferredMarkerNote: A device entry is deferred if and only if it contains BOTH strings. Requiring the basis as well as the word means a device set cannot be quietly parked without naming the decision that parked it.
assertionScopeContract.authorityNote: scopeClause is normative and machine-checked in both artifacts. The remaining prose in an assertion is explanatory and carries no scope: it may not introduce a target that is neither in scope nor a declared mention, which is the only way explanatory prose could smuggle a scope back in.

openConstraints.statement: The macOS packet-tunnel system extension runs as root in a non-user context. The Data Protection Keychain is available only to code running in a user context, and keychain access groups share items between programs running as the SAME user. The .spec/security-privacy.md design — private keys and passphrases in the Data Protection Keychain shared through one access group with the packet tunnel extension — therefore CANNOT work between the macOS host and the macOS provider. It works unchanged on iOS.
openConstraints.corroboration: Observed 2026-07-28 on this Mac. (a) Two shipping Developer ID packet-tunnel system extensions ship com.apple.security.temporary-exception.files.absolute-path.read-write entries for /private/var/root/Library/Group Containers/ (Tailscale, Surfshark) — direct evidence that a root provider's group container is not the user's. (b) Surfshark's provider carries a temporary-exception path for /Library/Keychains/, i.e. the FILE-BASED System keychain, not the Data Protection Keychain. (c) PureVPN's providers carry keychain-access-groups outright. Together these indicate the real-world macOS pattern is a file-based/System keychain or an IPC seed, not a shared Data Protection Keychain access group.

Matrix consequence: macos.provider keychain-access-groups is settled prohibited (rule K1), not pending. appGroupLeastPrivilegeRule.statement: com.apple.security.application-groups is granted only to a target whose OWN currently selected design uses one of the grants the entitlement actually confers on that platform. A possible future transport, a spec sentence, the shape of a target it resembles, and the cost of a second portal sitting are none of them a function. On iOS the two production targets qualify. The iOS probe pair does not: its own contract names no shared-container function, and G4 tests the target's own design, never an inherited one. On macOS no target qualifies today, so the key is prohibited on every macOS target, production and probe alike.
appGroupLeastPrivilegeRule.surveyBasis: The entitlement's macOS effect is not a matter of opinion: it is two sandbox-array-entitlement blocks in the system App Sandbox profile. Both were read in full at /System/Library/Sandbox/Profiles/application.sb on macOS 26.5 (25F71) rather than inferred from documentation. They are the only two occurrences of the key in that profile.

Directly corroborated: two shipping packet-tunnel system extensions on this Mac ship temporary-exception.files.absolute-path.read-write entries for /private/var/root/Library/Group Containers/, which is what you author when you need to cross that boundary.

App Store-delivered group content. This project ships development and Developer ID on macOS and never the Mac App Store (.spec/platform-distribution.md), so the path is never populated.

The XPC channel, and the only grant that ever made the macOS App Group look load-bearing. TASK-260728-7ii1xz evaluated a custom XPC Mach service as candidate C and REJECTED it: it requires an exception entitlement that rule X1 puts under review, and it is dominated by the selected candidate D. With no XPC service there is no prefix to authorize.

POSIX shared memory and semaphores in a group-prefixed namespace. This one does cross the root/user boundary and is easy to miss. No candidate transport proposed it, the accepted M1 lifecycle contract does not use it, and it is named here so that a future design cannot claim the entitlement was withheld without the option being seen.

appGroupLeastPrivilegeRule.privateContainerFinding: TASK-260728-7ii1xz amendment M6 left the rows granted on the grounds that 'a private root-context container may still have uses this task did not survey'. Surveyed here, and the answer is no. (appsandbox-container-common) and (appsandbox-container-macos) at application.sb:107-108 are UNCONDITIONAL - they are not inside any (when (entitlement ...)) form - so a sandboxed target already has its own private container, derived from the application_container_id sandbox parameter, without any App Group entitlement. The only thing a group container adds over the container the provider already has is SHARING, and sharing is precisely what the root/user split breaks. A private group container is therefore strictly redundant, not merely unused.
appGroupLeastPrivilegeRule.selectedTransport: TASK-260728-7ii1xz selected candidate D: the provider owns a file-based system-domain keychain item, seeded once from the containing app over NETunnelProviderSession.sendProviderMessage, with the non-secret profile snapshot carried in providerConfiguration. Keychain, NE app message, providerConfiguration - none of the three is an App Group mechanism.
appGroupLeastPrivilegeRule.iOSUnaffected: On iOS the host and the appex run as the same user in the same context, so the group container and UserDefaults suite are genuinely shared and the .spec/architecture.md:111 design holds unchanged for PRODUCTION. ios.host and ios.provider keep the entitlement as required.
appGroupLeastPrivilegeRule.reopensOnly: This row reopens if, and only if, one of three things becomes true, each of which is a grant in the survey above rather than a general appeal to App Groups: (a) the macOS host-to-provider channel becomes a group-prefixed Mach service, i.e. the XPC candidate is revived; (b) it becomes a group-prefixed POSIX IPC object; or (c) the provider is moved out of root into a user context, which would make the group container genuinely shared. It does NOT reopen because a spec sentence mentions App Groups, because a shipping third-party product carries the key, or to spare a portal sitting. Reopening is an amendment under section 11, naming which of (a), (b) or (c) became true.
appGroupLeastPrivilegeRule.ceremonyCostIsZero: Withholding introduces no new human ceremony, which removes the operational argument verdict 03 rejected. The four iOS App IDs are already in c1AuthorizationScope.explicitlyNotAuthorized under ADR-024, so iOS provisioning already requires a later portal sitting that C1 does not cover. The App Group record is allocated at that sitting, alongside the iOS App IDs that are its only consumers. Nothing that C1 could have granted today is needed today. (r6: this sentence counted r4's two records until rule S1's count scan caught it - the third instance of the stale-summary class reviewer verdict 05 F1 named, and the one neither the reviewer nor r5 had spotted.)

TASK-260715-1jckn0 (iOS) and TASK-260715-1r0fxv (macOS) both scope their probe to the NETunnelProviderManager lifecycle plus a versioned app message, and neither names a shared container, so no probe target on either platform is granted an App Group. If a probe is meant to prove that a capability can be provisioned at all, that is a VERIFICATION deliverable and must be written into the probe task as an acceptance criterion first; the entitlement then follows the criterion, not the other way round.

keychainScopeRule.statement: On macOS the file-based (system-domain) keychain is controlled by per-item SecAccess ACLs. keychain-access-groups applies only to the Data Protection Keychain, which is unavailable outside a user context. A root-context provider targeting the system-domain keychain therefore never needs this entitlement, and the presence of the key in a shipping third-party provider is not evidence that it functions.
keychainScopeRule.replaces: The amendmentRule formerly carried on targets[macos.provider].entitlements[keychain-access-groups]. That rule said the row would be amended to required if the resolved transport gave the provider direct keychain access. Its antecedent is now TRUE - candidate D does give the provider direct keychain access - while its consequent is FALSE, because the file-based keychain has no access groups. Left in place it was a live instruction to re-grant the row on exactly the reasoning TASK-260728-7ii1xz refutes.
keychainScopeRule.reopeningCondition: The macos.provider row reopens only if the provider is moved into a user context, not merely because it touches a keychain.
keychainScopeRule.shippingProductsAreNotEvidence: PureVPN's packet-tunnel system extensions carry keychain-access-groups. Under this rule that observation may not be used to argue the row back open: a key present in a signed bundle is not proof that the mechanism it names is the one the process uses.
keychainScopeRule.source: Apple TN3137 'On Mac keychain APIs and implementations'; TASK-260728-7ii1xz_macos-credential-transport-decision.md sections 4-5 and 7.
keychainScopeRule.hostScope: K1 governs the macOS PROVIDER only. It says nothing about the macOS host, which does run in a user context and does use the Data Protection Keychain, and that silence is what let r4 keep a shared access group on macos.host with no second member to share with. Rule K2 closes it: sharing is the entitlement's only function, so a host with no co-member is served by its default access group. Reviewer verdict 04 F1.
keychainScopeRule.osFloorScope: K1's 'never needs this entitlement' clause is unconditional and stays that way - the Data Protection Keychain has no meaning in a root context on any OS version. Rule K3 owns that version scope: it names the macOS 15.0 floor, names the owner that closes it, and pre-authorizes the temporary FILE exception an absent floor grant would require. That exception is not this entitlement, so arming it never reopens this row. Reviewer verdict 08 F1.

The minimum-macOS lane gains one credential-free static check: read /System/Library/Sandbox/Profiles/application.sb on the macos-15 runner and record whether a process holding com.apple.developer.networking.networkextension is granted file-read* and file-write* on the /Library/Keychains subpath, together with the com.apple.securityd.xpc and com.apple.SecurityServer Mach lookups. Absent means arm register entry X1-C1 under rule K3; present means retire it. This is a read of the runner's own system files - no credential, no signing, no portal access, and no new board element. TASK-260715-1o9wjz consumes the same answer at runtime, because an absent grant surfaces there as a provider-context failure rather than as a build finding.

keychainLeastPrivilegeRule.statement: keychain-access-groups is granted only to a target that must share a Data Protection Keychain item with a NAMED second target in this contract. A target that only reads and writes its own items is already served by the default access group the signing toolchain gives it, so the entitlement would add signed authority with no consumer. On iOS the host and the appex are two such members and both are granted. On macOS there is no second member today, so the key is prohibited on all four macOS targets.
keychainLeastPrivilegeRule.defaultAccessGroupLaw: The system forms each app's access-group array as the keychain-access-groups entitlement array first, then the application identifier, then the app groups; the FIRST element is the default group that keychain services uses when a caller names none. Two consequences this contract depends on. (a) A target with no keychain-access-groups entitlement still has a private default group equal to <TeamID>.<bundle id>, so withholding never costs a target access to its own items. (b) Withholding MOVES the default: macos.host's default group changes from 262RZ595FP.works.relux.tunnel.shared under r4 to 262RZ595FP.works.relux.tunnel.mac under r5. A consumer must not paper that over with an explicit kSecAttrAccessGroup naming the shared group - on macOS the correct call names no access group at all, and naming the shared one returns errSecMissingEntitlement.
keychainLeastPrivilegeRule.sharingIsTheOnlyFunction: The entitlement confers exactly one thing beyond the default group: membership of a group that another target can also join. It does not unlock the Data Protection Keychain, does not change item durability, and does not survive anything the default group does not. Any argument for granting it that does not name a second reading target is therefore an argument for something the entitlement does not do.
keychainLeastPrivilegeRule.relationToK1: K1 explains why the macOS PROVIDER can never be a member: the file-based system-domain keychain it uses has no access groups. K2 is the rule K1 did not cover - why the macOS HOST, which does use the Data Protection Keychain, still gets no custom group. Reviewer verdict 04 F1 named exactly that gap: the provider-side test was applied and the host-side one was not.
keychainLeastPrivilegeRule.reopeningCondition: Per-row, in targets[].entitlements['keychain-access-groups'].reopensOnly. A row reopens only on a named second member, never on convenience or cross-platform symmetry.
keychainLeastPrivilegeRule.source: Apple, Sharing access to keychain items among a collection of apps (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/security/sharing-access-to-keychain-items-among-a-collection-of-apps); Apple TN3137, On Mac keychain APIs and implementations (https://developer.apple.com/documentation/technotes/tn3137-on-mac-keychains). Both fetched 2026-07-28.
keychainLeastPrivilegeRule.settledByDecisionNotOmission: Every withheld keychain row states its own reopening condition, on both platforms and in both families. r1-r4 left the four probe rows prohibited with no such condition, which made them settled by omission - indistinguishable from an oversight, and reopenable by anyone who read the silence as 'nobody considered it'. Rule R31 now rejects a withheld row that states no reopening condition, which is the same discipline rule G4 already applies to App Groups.

consumerDependencyContract.statement: Every board element this contract names as an obligation owner or an affected task is a DECLARED CONSUMER. A declared consumer must (a) appear in `consumers` and (b) transitively depend on TASK-260715-ypo7yo on the live board. Rules A1 and P1 pin the two consumers that carry a revision label, because a label can go stale. Every other consumer carries no label, so the only thing standing between it and being authored against an unaccepted matrix is the dependency edge — and a missing edge fails silently, because nothing reads a prose consumer list.
consumerDependencyContract.history: Found by this task in r9 during a self-audit after the r8 handoff; no reviewer verdict reported it. r1 wrote the `consumers` list as prose and r4–r8 grew it while the board DAG was never compared against it. Three declared consumers had no dependency path to this task at all, and four elements carrying obligations were absent from the list. This is the verdict-05 F2 class one field over: verdict 05 checked what a consumer SAYS, rules A1 and P1 check which revision it names, and nothing checked WHEN it runs.
declaredConsumerSources: consumers[] — every element id in each entry
openConstraints[].affects[] — each entry is an element id
downstreamConsequences[].owner — every element id in the owner string; the spec-amendment owner is written as prose wrapped around an id
any other string in this contract — see mentionCoverageRule
consumerDependencyContract.mentionCoverageRule: The derived set is NOT those named paths alone. Rule D1 scans EVERY string in this contract for an element id, because an obligation can be assigned in a sentence rather than in a list: TASK-260717-xempiv owned the Sparkle nested-code re-signing obligation for five revisions from inside two prose fields and appeared in no list, and TASK-260715-35nc5m owned the legacy migration decision from `legacy.migrationDecisionOwner` for eight. Every id found anywhere must be a declared consumer, a registered exemption, or this contract's own owner. There is no mention-only class: a contract that names a task names it for a reason.
consumerDependencyContract.reachabilityRule: TRANSITIVE, not direct. A declared consumer satisfies D1 if any chain of blockedBy edges from it reaches TASK-260715-ypo7yo. Requiring a direct edge from each of twenty consumers would flatten a DAG the board already orders correctly — thirteen of them reach this task through TASK-260715-3jloqy, which is the honest shape, because they consume the matrix through the portal state it produces.
consumerDependencyContract.whyNotAStatusCheck: A `done` consumer is not automatically exempt. Being finished is not evidence that it ran with this contract in hand — it is evidence that it ran, which is the failure mode this rule exists to catch. Only an UPSTREAM element is exempt, and the board gate verifies the upstream claim rather than accepting it.

exemptions.reason: It BLOCKS this task: the macOS credential transport decision is an input to rules K1, K2 and G4, and its r2 amendment packet M1–M7 was applied here in r4. Requiring it to depend on this task would be a cycle. It is also `done`, but that is not the basis — the basis is the direction of the edge.

boardChange.why: One edge, three gaps. TASK-260715-29ws8l already blocks TASK-260715-1o9wjz and TASK-260715-3f4lxy, so ordering it after this contract orders all three. The edge is semantically real, not a scheduling trick: 29ws8l AC2 requires it to specify what travels in 'App Group and providerConfiguration data' and AC4 requires it to specify 'Keychain accessibility, access group' — on macOS rule G4 prohibits the App Group on every target and rule K2 prohibits the keychain access group on every target, so authoring 29ws8l without this matrix reproduces exactly the iOS-only assumption OC-1 was raised against.
boardChange.cycleCheck: The whole blockedBy graph was checked for cycles with this edge added before it was written: none. TASK-260715-ypo7yo depends only on TASK-260728-7ii1xz, which depends on nothing.
boardChange.footprint: One dependency edge added. No board element created, deleted, re-parented, or re-scoped by this rule.

boardGate.graphNote: Both element types are read. A bug can carry a dependency edge, so reading tasks alone would compute a closure over a subgraph and could call a consumer unreachable — or reachable — on incomplete data.
requires: every declared consumer resolves to a live board element
every declared consumer that is not a registered exemption transitively depends on TASK-260715-ypo7yo
every registered exemption is genuinely UPSTREAM: this task transitively depends on it
the derived mention set equals the declared consumer set plus the exemptions plus this contract's own owner, in both directions

consumerDependencyContract.gate: TASK-260715-ypo7yo_check-portal-consumer.py adds a third block, rule D1, which reads the live dependency graph and computes the transitive closure. validate_matrix.py cannot read the board; R37 checks only that this pin is well formed, that the mention set and the consumer list agree, and that every exemption carries an allowed basis and a reason.
consumerDependencyContract.source: Self-audit, r9. The consumer list in this contract, openConstraints, downstreamConsequences, and the live board dependency graph. ADR-027 (deferral is `blocked`, never an unlinked backlog item) is the same principle applied to deferral rather than to consumption.
consumerDependencyContract.whyBlockersAreNotNamed: The two unrelated blockers that stood in these chains are described rather than named. Naming them would make them mentions, and rule D1's own mentionCoverageRule would then require them to be declared consumers of a contract they do not consume — a rule that manufactures its own violations by describing them. The board gate reads the real edges, so nothing is lost by not spelling the ids here.

numericClaimContract.statement: A count, or an enumerated key list, stated in prose about an entitlement allowlist is a PROJECTION of the target rows plus the signing-generated table. Each one is registered here and recomputed by the gate in both artifacts. A number written out by hand is a claim nothing checks.
numericClaimContract.history: Found by this task in r9. §9.1 records the class biting once already: r3's prose said the macos.host development allowlist was 'exactly seven keys' over a list of ten, and r4 corrected it by hand to nine. r5 then moved it again to eight, when rule K2 withdrew keychain-access-groups from every macOS target. Three revisions, three different numbers, corrected by hand each time. r6 built a count scan for App Group RECORD counts (rule S1's recordCountClaimRule) after verdict 05 exposed a stale one, and stopped there — so the other live count class stayed unchecked in both artifacts for three more revisions.
numericClaimContract.derivation: allowlist(target, channel) = { entitlement keys whose status is in entitlementClassification.authoredStatuses } ∪ signingGenerated[platform].always ∪ (channel == development ? signingGenerated[platform].developmentChannelOnly : ∅). This is the same expression §9.1 renders and the same one assertions A10a–A10d apply; N1 makes the prose numbers agree with it instead of restating it.
numericClaimContract.spelling: Every live claim spells its number as an English word, which is why the gate owns a word table rather than matching digits: 'eight' and '8' are the same number and only one of them appears in these artifacts.

renderedClaims.template: The `macos.host` allowlist is **{0}** keys on `development`, **{1}** on `developer-id`
the allowlist resolves to exactly **{0}** keys — **{1} authored** plus **{2}** the toolchain injects

keyList.note: The fenced block immediately after the N1-3 development claim enumerates the allowlist one key per line. The gate compares the SET of keys in that block against the derived allowlist in both directions, so a row added to macos.host that nobody rendered, or a key left rendered after its row was withdrawn, both fail. This is the check that would have caught the r3 defect at the time: the number and the list disagreed, and only a human noticed.

claims.note: §13 is excluded from the coverage SCAN because it quotes numbers that were wrong at the time and must stay wrong. The r9 entry states a live derived count anyway, so it is registered instead of hidden behind the section exclusion. A registered claim is recomputed wherever it lives; the section exclusions govern the scan, not the derivation.

coverageScan.requires: every hit must fall inside a registered claim's rendered text, or be listed in excludedPhrases with a reason. An unregistered count fails closed.
coverageScan.excludedJsonNote: Two kinds. Append-only history — revisionLog and the `history` / `staleClaimsFound` fields — where a past count is a true historical statement, exactly as rule A1 excludes `notes` and rule S1 excludes revisionLog from its own scan. And this rule's own register, because `claims` and `coverageScan` necessarily contain the templates and the excluded phrases the scan is looking for; a rule that flagged its own definition could never pass.
coverageScan.excludedDocSectionNote: §13 records how each verdict was verified and necessarily quotes the numbers that were wrong at the time; they must NOT be updated to the current allowlist size. Excluding a whole section opens a hole for a LIVE count written into it, which is why the r9 entry's own derived count is registered as N1-4 rather than left to the exclusion.

excludedPhrases.phrase: r3's prose claimed "exactly seven keys" while the list beneath it held ten
excludedPhrases.reason: The §9.1 paragraph that records the r3 defect. Quoting a wrong number is how the correction is documented; deriving it would erase the correction.

coverageScan.knownBound: The scan is shape-specific: it finds `<number> keys`. The developer-id claims in §9.1 and in downstreamConsequences render the number without the word 'keys' adjacent in one case, so the scan alone would not have found them — REGISTRATION found them, because the gate requires each registered rendered claim to be present verbatim. Stated rather than left as an implied completeness claim: N1 does not guarantee that no unregistered count of any shape exists anywhere, it guarantees that every registered one is derived and that no `<number> keys` claim is unregistered.
coverageScan.excludedDocPreamble: Everything before the first '## ' heading is the document's change-history preamble, the prose twin of revisionLog. Each revision's blockquote describes what it changed, including numbers that were correct then and are not now.

numericClaimContract.relationToS1: Complementary, not overlapping. Rule S1's recordCountClaimRule owns App Group RECORD counts at registered paths; N1 owns entitlement ALLOWLIST counts and the rendered key list. Neither scans the other's shape, and R38 checks that N1's registered paths do not collide with S1's recordCountClaimPaths, so a count cannot end up owned twice with two derivations.
numericClaimContract.source: Self-audit, r9. §9.1 of the rationale document, which records the r3 and r4 instances; the macos.host target row; entitlementClassification.signingGenerated.

keychainSandboxFloorRule.statement: The conclusion that the macOS provider needs no keychain-related entitlement rests on a BASE OS SANDBOX GRANT, which is an OS-version-scoped fact about the running system rather than an invariant of this contract. It holds on the OS versions where it has actually been read. On any supported version below that it is UNVERIFIED, and this contract models it as unresolved instead of settling it by silence.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.verifiedOn: macOS 26.5 (25F71). /System/Library/Sandbox/Profiles/application.sb lines 792-793 grant file-read* and file-write* on the /Library/Keychains subpath to any process holding com.apple.developer.networking.networkextension, and lines 655-656 allow the com.apple.securityd.xpc and com.apple.SecurityServer Mach lookups unconditionally. Re-read and confirmed unchanged for r10.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.unverifiedAtFloor: macOS 15.0 - the binding deployment floor for generated targets, set by .spec/platform-distribution.md 'Minimum platform policy' and selected exactly in .research/260720_task-260715-3r0993-project-generator-deployment-target-policy.md, which also names macos-15 as the minimum hosted CI lane. No macOS 15 host, virtual machine, installer, or SDK-resident sandbox profile exists in this task's environment - only Xcode 26.5 and macOS 26 SDKs - so the floor profile could not be read here. Apple does not document application.sb contents, so no secondary source closes it either. This is a stated gap, not an inference.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.whyItMatters: This matrix is the source for generated entitlements and for the automated allowlist checks. If the floor's base profile does NOT carry the grant, the provider needs a temporary FILE EXCEPTION to reach the System-keychain transport TASK-260728-7ii1xz selected. With no model for that case, the required exception would be rejected as an unreviewed relaxation under rule X1 and assertion A10a, on a supported OS - a silent rejection of a real requirement. Reviewer verdict 08 F1.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.resolutionOwner: TASK-260715-1uxx3i - it already owns the credential-free Apple build matrix whose minimum-macOS lane runs on the macos-15 hosted runner, and reading /System/Library/Sandbox/Profiles/application.sb there is a credential-free static read squarely inside its AC2 static checks. No board element is created for this: the floor lane already exists, and it already reaches this contract transitively through TASK-260715-uyju7n on the live board.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.runtimeConsumer: TASK-260715-1o9wjz - the provider-context resolver whose macOS path actually opens the System keychain. Its provider-context tests are where an absent grant surfaces as a runtime failure rather than as a build finding, so it is the second place the answer lands.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.ifGrantAbsentAtFloor: Arm register entry X1-C1: com.apple.security.temporary-exception.files.absolute-path.read-write valued /Library/Keychains/ on macos.provider only, on its two macOS channels. Arming is PRE-AUTHORIZED by this revision, so the exception is a reviewed one the moment the evidence exists and is never an unreviewed relaxation under rule X1 - the review is recorded here, the evidence belongs to the owner. It is an amendment under section 11 that moves the row status and the register entry and changes nothing else.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.ifGrantPresentAtFloor: Record the floor evidence against this rule and retire entry X1-C1. The macos.provider keychain decision then needs no further change: the row stays prohibited under rule K1, on the reason K1 already gives.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.notAPortalCapability: A temporary file exception is a signing-time App Sandbox entitlement. It is not an App ID capability, carries no portal record, and cannot be created or authorized in the Developer portal. Arming it therefore adds nothing to Ceremony C1, whose authorized entries stay exactly as c1AuthorizationScope states them.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.productEvidenceIsNotProof: Re-read on this Mac for r10. Surfshark's packet-tunnel system extension declares LSMinimumSystemVersion 10.15 and ships com.apple.security.temporary-exception.files.absolute-path.read-write covering /private/var/db/mds/, /Library/Keychains/ and a further private path; PureVPN's two providers declare 10.15 and carry keychain-access-groups; Tailscale's declares 12.4 and carries no keychain entitlement at all. A support range opening at 10.15 spans OS versions this project does not support, and a bundled defensive path set is not a targeted floor fix, so none of the three establishes either necessity or redundancy at macOS 15.0. Rule K1's clause runs in both directions here: a key present in a shipping bundle is not proof the mechanism functions, and a key absent from one is not proof it is unnecessary.
keychainSandboxFloorRule.source: Reviewer verdict 08 F1. /System/Library/Sandbox/Profiles/application.sb on macOS 26.5 (25F71); .spec/platform-distribution.md minimum platform policy; Apple TN3137.
